actions.action: Represent New IP as a failed but observable standards agenda-setting attempt, not as a captured/adopted global standard.
Reopen state tasking only on direct instruction/governance/communications linking MIIT to specific corporate contribution decisions.
Preserve Huawei technical rationale and IETF/ICANN objections side-by-side; do not infer political intent from architecture alone.

axes.gap: Joint sponsorship is observable; separate evidence of MIIT tasking each corporate co-sponsor was not found in the bounded run.
axes.question: Is state-industry joint sponsorship directly observable, and does it prove tasking/control?
Can New IP be explained as a bona fide technical research agenda rather than a control project?
Did the proposal move through an institutional standards process and trigger organized counter-mobilization?
Was New IP/FVCN adopted as ITU-T work/standard in the bounded period?
Does participation in ITU standardization itself establish capture, ingérence or malign intent?

The MIIT/firm co-signature proves that the Chinese state tasked or controlled every corporate co-proponent.
claims.gap: Joint sponsorship/coordination is established at contribution level; tasking relationship for each firm is not established.

claims.claim: New IP was merely a technical research initiative with no material governance implications.
New IP was an adopted ITU replacement for TCP/IP or a captured global standard.
Formal standards participation can function as institutional influence/agenda-setting even when the proposal is rejected.
Opposition to New IP was simply geopolitical resistance with no technical basis.
New IP proponents had a proven malign political intent to centralize surveillance/control.
claims.gap: Technical/governance risk is documented; proponent intent to enable political control is not proven by the inspected corpus.

rejection != absence of attempted institutional influence

facts.subject: New IP C83 co-proponents
facts.value: ITU-T catalog metadata lists Contribution 83, New IP, Shaping Future Network, with China Mobile, China Unicom, Huawei Technologies and China Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) as sources.

facts.subject: New IP entered formal ITU-T process
facts.value: TSAG considered a New IP tutorial and contribution proposing analysis of current challenges and a future-network development path; ITU-T then transmitted the material to IETF/IAB for comment ahead of WTSA.

facts.subject: Huawei stated rationale
facts.value: Huawei describes New IP as a technology-research initiative for future industrial/social network requirements and states that it does not define control mechanisms or centralized top-down Internet control.

facts.subject: IETF technical opposition
facts.value: The IETF said it had seen no evidence for a monolithic top-down New IP, identified unsupported/incorrect premises, and argued that replacing the existing IP stack wholesale would harm interoperability and create network islands.

facts.subject: Continued New IP standardization proposals
facts.value: ITU-T SG13 catalog records a contribution titled New IP potential standards in 2021 from China Mobile, China Telecom and Huawei, showing continued effort beyond the September 2019 TSAG proposal.

facts.subject: France/EU formal counter-contribution
facts.value: A formal SG13 contribution co-sponsored by France, the European Commission, multiple European states, GSMA and RIPE NCC urged that no New IP-related work-item/question decisions be taken before analysis and argued that IETF should lead Internet-architecture development.

facts.subject: Broad coalition sought non-adoption
facts.value: A later SG13 contribution co-sponsored by France, EU actors, European states, ETNO, GSMA and RIPE NCC said the case for New IP/FVCN questions had not been made and proposed that the proposed questions not go forward for adoption.

facts.subject: Sustained counter-mobilization
facts.value: RIPE NCC documents a sequence of New IP responses in TSAG, SG11 and SG13 during 2020, while its contemporaneous update describes the questions as contested and the label shifting toward Future Vertical Communication Networks.

facts.subject: ICANN technical assessment
facts.value: ICANN OCTO described New IP as incomplete work in progress, analyzed variable-length addressing, ManyNets and other elements, and assessed incompatibility risks with the deployed IPv4/IPv6 Internet.

facts.subject: ICANN governance/security concern
facts.value: ICANN OCTO assessed that proposed strong regulatory binding between IP address and user could make pervasive monitoring easier; this is an ICANN technical-risk assessment, not proof of the proponents political intent.

facts.subject: New IP study-group outcome
facts.value: ICANN government-engagement reporting states that New IP proposals were not accepted at ITU-T study-group level in 2020.

facts.subject: WTSA outcome
facts.value: The same ICANN report states that because New IP proposals were not accepted at study-group level, they were not accepted at WTSA-20.

facts.subject: Opposition was technical and governance-oriented
facts.value: Independent IETF and European/sector-member contributions objected on interoperability, duplication, technical-merit, multistakeholder-process and economic-risk grounds; opposition was not merely geopolitical labeling.

facts.subject: Material narrative divergence
facts.value: Huawei framed New IP as open technical research under normal consensus processes and rejected centralized-control interpretations, while IETF and ICANN documented substantial architectural/interoperability/governance concerns. The disagreement itself is established; malign intent is not.

facts.subject: Proposal did not become the proposed ITU work program
facts.value: The bounded New IP/FVCN proposal encountered organized opposition and was not accepted into the next ITU-T study-period/WTSA outcome in the form tested here.

facts.subject: European government coordination around standards response
facts.value: RIPE 80 minutes record German government support for bottom-up multistakeholder Internet development and coordination with German ITU representatives and others, illustrating that the counter-response itself also involved state coordination.

leads.evidence_excerpt: MIIT + China Mobile + China Unicom + Huawei are listed as sources of Contribution 83.
leads.lead: New IP was formally co-sponsored by a Chinese ministry and telecom firms in an ITU-T contribution, making state-industry coalition observable at the proposal level.

leads.evidence_excerpt: future industrial requirements; research initiative; no control mechanisms; consensus process.
leads.lead: The proponent narrative supplies a legitimate technical rationale and explicitly denies centralized-control intent; this is a required symmetry control.
leads.locator: New IP initiative sections Why/What/What it is not

leads.evidence_excerpt: no evidence for monolithic New IP; top-down replacement would harm interoperability.
leads.lead: IETF formally contested the need and architecture, creating a standards-body counter-case rather than a geopolitical allegation alone.

leads.evidence_excerpt: case not made; significant concerns; questions should not go forward for adoption.
leads.lead: France/EU/industry/RIPE jointly sought non-adoption of the proposed New IP/FVCN questions.

leads.evidence_excerpt: New IP proposals were not accepted at ITU-T study group level in 2020, and thus were not accepted at WTSA-20.
leads.lead: The tested proposal failed to cross the adoption edge: not accepted at study-group level and therefore not at WTSA-20.

CREDO.truth_ceiling: The strongest closed result is attempted standards agenda-setting plus counter-mobilization and non-adoption; not capture or proven malign intent.

perspectives.best_case: New IP responds to future industrial requirements through normal SDO consensus and is not a control architecture.
IETF/ICANN identify duplication, interoperability and architectural risks; existing IP can evolve without top-down replacement.
Joint state-industry proposals can be strategic agenda-setting in standards venues, but this case ended in counter-mobilization and non-adoption rather than capture.
